title: Do good, avoid evil (ST I-II.94.2)
hookLine: the first principle of the natural law

lines: AN ARGUMENT AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.
cards: Two sisters at a kitchen table are arguing about whether to tell their cousin the hard truth about her new boyfriend. One says tell her now. The other says wait, it isn't our place.
But underneath sits one thing neither says out loud, because neither needs to: both are trying to find the good thing to do. Nobody at that table argues for the bad option.
Thomas Aquinas would call that buried agreement the first principle at work.

teach.h: THINKING ABOUT WHAT IS, AND WHAT TO DO.
teach.b: Where does the natural law start? Thomas compares two kinds of thinking. When we think about what is, the first rule is that a thing can't both be and not be at the same time; every other argument leans on that.
When we think about what to do, there has to be a first rule too, and Thomas finds it in the meaning of good.
Good is what things seek. So the first principle of the practical mind is this: good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided. It sounds almost too simple.

That's the point. It isn't a conclusion you argue your way to; it's known in itself, like knowing a whole is bigger than its part. Back on day three hundred ten, conscience said the same words: do good, avoid evil.
Everything else in the natural law hangs from it. Thomas shows how it unfolds, from what people are drawn to by nature. Like everything that exists, we're drawn to keep on living.
Like the animals, to bring up our young. As reasoning creatures, to know the truth about God and to live with others in society.
So the natural law says: protect life, care for children, shun ignorance, don't harm the people you live among.
Thomas leans on a line from the Psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "The light of thy countenance O Lord, is signed upon us."
He reads it as the light of reason, stamped on us like a seal.
Paul says people without the written law "shew the work of the law written in their hearts." For Thomas, the moral life doesn't start with a rulebook. It starts with a light already on.

how: Catholic moral teaching speaks of a natural law that human reason can know, and the Catechism, drawing on Thomas, describes it as the light of understanding placed in us by God.

o: the first rule of action, known by itself
a command from the Ten Commandments
a rule you reach after a long argument

games.q: the first principle — tap the pairs.

s: for Thomas, do good, avoid evil is something you have to prove
he says it's known in itself, like knowing a whole is bigger than its part.
Thomas reads the natural law from what people are drawn to by nature
keeping alive, raising the young, knowing the truth about God, living with others.

games.q: you're Thomas. a student asks what the very first rule of the practical mind is, the one every other rule leans on. what do you say?
o: good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided.
do whatever brings the most pleasure.
games.why: Thomas grounds it in what good means: good is what things seek. so: do good, avoid evil. everything else in the natural law hangs from it.

practice: Look ahead at the rest of today and find one specific good you could do, a call you've put off, a thank-you you owe, and one specific harm you could steer around, a sharp comment forming, a shortcut that isn't honest.
Hold both in mind, side by side, and if you pray, ask for help with each.

wordCard.voice: Do good. The start of Thomas's first principle: good is to be done and pursued, evil avoided. Everything else hangs from it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the first principle. Under every hard choice: which way is the good? See you tomorrow.
